article_title: Obstetric simulation for undergraduate medical education: how to improve students' self-confidence and expectation according to gender.
citation: Nomura Roseli Mieko Yamamoto, Reis Fabiana Medeiros D., Gonçalves Amanda Menezes, de Proença Carolina Matos. (2023). Obstetric simulation for undergraduate medical education: how to improve students’ self-confidence and expectation according to gender. Revista da Associação Médica Brasileira. https://doi.org/10.1590/1806-9282.20221625
title: 26-item five-subscale self-confidence questionnaire adapted from Scholz et al.
description: A self-assessment questionnaire based on the instrument proposed by Scholz et al., translated into Brazilian Portuguese and adapted to clerkship medical students, using a 5-point Likert scale. "The self-assessment questionnaire contains 26 items divided into five subscales: comprehension and preparation (5 items), knowledge of procedures (5 items), motivation (6 items), expectation (4 items), and interest (6 items)." Internal consistency was assessed with Cronbach's alpha, reported as 0.823 (95% lower confidence limit: 0.781), with six reversed variables.
requirements: Administered before the first simulation session and at the end of the rotation
Six variables reversed prior to Cronbach's alpha analysis
constraints: Adapted specifically to medical students in the obstetric clerkship context
target_learning_goals: measuring self-confidence in obstetric procedures, skills, and expectations
examples: The same questionnaire was applied before the beginning of the first simulation session and at the end of the rotation
key_sources: Nomura Roseli Mieko Yamamoto, Reis Fabiana Medeiros D., Gonçalves Amanda Menezes, de Proença Carolina Matos. (2023). Obstetric simulation for undergraduate medical education: how to improve students’ self-confidence and expectation according to gender. Revista da Associação Médica Brasileira. https://doi.org/10.1590/1806-9282.20221625

article_title: Conversion of extrinsic into intrinsic motivation and computer based testing (CBT).
citation: Hariri-Akbari M, Shokrvash B, Mahmoodi F, Jahanjoo-Aminabad F, Yousefi B, Azabdaftari F. (2018). Conversion of extrinsic into intrinsic motivation and computer based testing (CBT). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1249-4
title: A 26-item SDT-based questionnaire measuring student motivation toward computer-based testing
description: The researchers prepared a questionnaire based on Self-Determination Theory to estimate the quality of motivation (intrinsic and extrinsic) for computer-based testing. It contained 26 items with a five-point Likert scale, adapted from a previous valid questionnaire and reviewed by five professors and students. Qualitative content validity retained all 26 items, and internal consistency measured by Cronbach's Alpha was 0.884.
requirements: Respondents complete the 26 five-point Likert items (strongly agree = 5 to strongly disagree = 1) in class sessions under supervision, requiring about 15-20 min
constraints: The computer related skills and literacy of the students were not evaluated before the distribution of the questionnaires
target_learning_goals: assessment of motivation quality (intrinsic vs extrinsic) toward computer-based testing
examples: Administered to 246 undergraduate paramedical students taking General English at Tabriz Medical Sciences University during fall 2013-2014
key_sources: Hariri-Akbari M, Shokrvash B, Mahmoodi F, Jahanjoo-Aminabad F, Yousefi B, Azabdaftari F. (2018). Conversion of extrinsic into intrinsic motivation and computer based testing (CBT). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1249-4

article_title: Awareness and knowledge among internal medicine house-staff for dose adjustment of commonly used medications in patients with CKD.
citation: Surana Sikander, Kumar Neeru, Vasudeva Amita, Shaikh Gulvahid, Jhaveri Kenar D., Shah Hitesh, Malieckal Deepa, Fogel Joshua, Sidhu Gurwinder, Rubinstein Sofia. (2017). Awareness and knowledge among internal medicine house-staff for dose adjustment of commonly used medications in patients with CKD. BMC Nephrology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12882-017-0443-7
title: 26-medication, 7-class CKD dose-adjustment survey instrument with GFR-threshold response options
description: A researcher-compiled survey instrument in which 'A list of 26 commonly used medications was compiled representing 7 different medication classes' — allergy, analgesic, cardiovascular, endocrine, gastrointestinal, neuropsychotropic, and rheumatologic. Each medication offered five response options, including needs adjustment at GFR below 90, 60, or 30 ml/min and 'I don't know'. Correct responses were scored one point each and aggregated to class and overall medication scores for the awareness and knowledge outcomes.
requirements: Administered to internal medicine house-staff across all levels of training surveyed in their fourth through sixth month of the training year
constraints: Medications were 'selected based on our perception of what was being commonly prescribed'
The authors 'did not allow participants to use any automated support such as mobile- or computer-based devices for guidance in adjusting prescription dose'
target_learning_goals: Assessing awareness and knowledge of renal medication dose adjustment
examples: The instrument yielded overall medication scores out of 26 for 341 participants, with class-level comparisons across PGY1, PGY2, and PGY3 groups via ANOVA, ANCOVA, and non-parametric tests.
key_sources: Surana Sikander, Kumar Neeru, Vasudeva Amita, Shaikh Gulvahid, Jhaveri Kenar D., Shah Hitesh, Malieckal Deepa, Fogel Joshua, Sidhu Gurwinder, Rubinstein Sofia. (2017). Awareness and knowledge among internal medicine house-staff for dose adjustment of commonly used medications in patients with CKD. BMC Nephrology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12882-017-0443-7
